definition: Introducing new ideas or methods that are original and break from the usual way.
example: The town's innovative bus schedule let riders request a pickup with a simple text message.
nuance: Innovative suggests a new method actually put into practice, while creative can describe imagination that never leaves the page.
prompt: A bakery owner is looking for ways to cut down on wasted food.
options: Her innovative plan turned day-old bread into crackers sold at half price.
Her innovative plan was to keep running the bakery exactly as bakeries always had.
The innovative baker copied the shop next door's waste policy word for word.
Innovative weeds spread through the bakery's herb garden and choked the basil.
reasons: Finding a fresh use for leftovers is an original solution to the waste problem.
Sticking with the traditional routine is the reverse of trying something new.
Copying someone else's idea exactly shows no originality.
This confuses the word with invasive, which describes things that spread harmfully.

practice.prompt: A science teacher wants her students to be more engaged during lab periods.
options: The students felt too innovative to stay awake, so most of them dozed off.
She tried an innovative approach where students designed their own experiments.
Her innovative lesson was last year's handout with a new date written at the top.
The innovative teacher refused to change a single step of the lab manual from 1985.
reasons: The word describes fresh ideas or methods, not a sleepy feeling.
Letting students invent experiments breaks from worksheet routines in a fresh way.
Reusing old material with a tiny change offers nothing new.
Refusing any change is the opposite of introducing new methods.
